That gift was given to him by Bill Allen, who was the CEO of an Alaskan oil company. And he said, you know, he's a whistleblower. He needs to be protected. And that was not true. This man had been denied whistleblower status by the Department of Justice before the Department of Justice approached me to let me know that it had this whistleblower letter. So, a lot of issues were percolating there. Ted Stevens was a United States Senator being prosecuted by the United States Department of Justice. Ted Stevens was a United States Senator being prosecuted by the United States Department of Justice. Ted Stevens was a United States Senator being prosecuted by the United States Department of Justice. The Public Integrity Section, in a public courtroom in the District of Columbia. It's a public trial. He has Sixth Amendment rights. The media had an interest. The community had an interest in learning what was going on. The whistleblower had an interest in keeping everything under seal. So, that was the first difficult post-drama issue to kind of balance all of these competing interests and try to figure out... The whistleblower had an interest in keeping everything under seal. So, that was the first difficult post-drama issue to kind of balance all of these competing interests and try to figure out... What the heck to do without getting reversed? So we had a hearing. There was no authority directly on point. What happens when someone's Sixth Amendment rights conflict with the alleged whistleblower rights? What happens? How should a judge resolve that? This was 10 years ago. I wrote a 29-page opinion. I resolved it in favor of the media, the community, and Senator Stevens. And I held that the complaint should be filed on the docket. But I was not insensitive to the rights of the whistleblower. And although I didn't say, I'm going to post these documents on the public docket in five days to give the government a chance to appeal, I didn't add that last part. But what I said was, I'm going to post the documents in five days so the government can figure it out if it wants to. And they want to challenge it. And the Court of Appeals, they could certainly challenge it. And the whistleblower, he was allowed to participate in this case. Agent Joy, he could challenge it. No one filed the challenge. So that was a hurl. You were over that. So what happened to that? I ordered that the unredacted complaint be produced to the defense. And suffice it to say, I wasn't pleased at all by this. I mean, this is the post-trial drama and that's the thing. This is the starting. And now we're aware that there's additional evidence that should have been produced to Senator Stevens and his team during the course of the trial. That revelation was a week before President Obama was to take his oath of office. And a new Attorney General, Eric Holder, was in place. You know, I had no intention to start this case again with a new Attorney General. It was an acting Attorney. It was an acting Attorney General by the name of McCasey. So, it seemed to me, the better part of wisdom was to order, directly order, Mr. McCasey to sign a declaration telling me everything he knew, everything any other attorney knew at the Department of Justice about this whistleblower and about all this evidence and to get it in to me within three or four days. Well, he thought otherwise. And, of course, they filed a petition that mandamus me with the circuit, which was fine. At least I got a reaction, which made me, and that's what I wanted.
